title: Why Does Your Ear Feel Clogged and Itchy After Swimming?

platforms.title: Why Does Your Ear Feel Clogged and Itchy After Swimming?
platforms.meta_description: A clogged, itchy ear after swimming isn't only leftover water - trapped moisture, cotton swabs, and earbuds all play a role in the irritation.
platforms.body_html:
If your ear feels clogged and itchy for days after a swim, it's easy to assume the water just hasn't drained yet. In most cases, though, the real driver is what's happening inside the ear canal once that water gets trapped - and a couple of everyday habits are often making it worse without you realizing it. Here's what's actually going on, and what tends to help.

Trapped Moisture Turns the Ear Canal Into a Breeding Ground

The skin lining the ear canal is normally protected by a thin, slightly acidic layer of earwax that keeps bacteria and fungi in check. Swimming, showering, or spending time in a humid environment can leave water sitting against that skin, washing away the protective layer and softening the tissue underneath. That warm, damp environment is exactly what bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus need to multiply, which is why swimmer's ear (otitis externa) tends to show up within a day or two of getting water trapped in the ear.

Cotton Swabs and Earbuds Make It Worse

Cotton swabs are one of the most common culprits behind ear canal irritation. Rather than removing wax, they usually push it deeper and scrape the thin skin lining the canal, creating tiny scratches that give bacteria an easy way in. Earbuds add another layer of risk: wearing them for hours at a time traps heat and moisture against the same skin, and the constant friction from insertion and removal irritates an already inflamed canal further.

Who Gets It More Often

The NHS describes an outer ear infection as something irritating the ear canal - eczema, water, or wearing earplugs - or a fungal or bacterial infection taking hold. That puts regular swimmers, long-time earplug and hearing aid wearers, and anyone with a skin condition around the ear in the group that sees it return year after year. Narrow or damaged ear canals and a lot of hair inside the canal also make wax harder to clear, which sets up the same cycle.

One symptom separates an outer ear infection from a middle ear one: with otitis externa, gently tugging the outer ear hurts. Most ear infections clear within about three days, though symptoms can last a week.

Three Myths Worth Dropping

  • Ears need cleaning out. The NHS is blunt: you cannot prevent earwax, and it is there to protect your ears from dirt and germs. Do not use fingers or cotton buds to remove it - that pushes it in and makes things worse.
  • Ear candles clear the wax. There is no evidence that ear candles or ear vacuums get rid of earwax, according to the NHS. If wax is genuinely blocking your ear, a pharmacist can suggest drops and some GP surgeries offer irrigation or microsuction.
  • Drops are always safe to try. Do not use ear drops if you have a hole in your eardrum (a perforated eardrum). And skip decongestants and antihistamines for an ear infection - there is no evidence they help.

What Actually Helps

  • Tilt your head and dry gently - After swimming or showering, tilt your head to each side to let water drain, then towel the outer ear dry. Do not insert anything into the canal itself.
  • Keep water and shampoo out - While an ear is irritated, keep water and shampoo out of it and do not swim until the infection has settled.
  • Skip the cotton swabs entirely - Earwax works its way out on its own; if it feels blocked, have it checked instead of digging at it.
  • Ask a pharmacist first - Pharmacies stock sprays and drops for outer ear problems, and a pharmacist can say which is suitable or point you to a GP.
  • Manage the pain sensibly - Paracetamol or ibuprofen help with earache; children under 16 should not take aspirin. Wipe discharge away with cotton wool rather than poking inside.
  • Give your earbuds a break - Swap to over-ear headphones when possible, and let your ears air out during long calls or workouts.

When to Get It Checked

See a GP if earache does not get better after three days, or if you keep getting ear infections. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 straight away if you feel generally unwell, have a very high temperature, swelling around the ear, fluid coming out of the ear, or a change in hearing or new hearing loss. The same applies if you are vomiting, feel dizzy, or have a severe sore throat.

Two groups should not wait it out: people with diabetes or a heart, lung, kidney or neurological condition, and anyone with a weakened immune system, for example during chemotherapy. In those cases the infection can spread beyond the canal, so early assessment matters.

Common Questions

Can I swim while my ear is sore? No. The NHS advises against swimming with an ear infection, because more water against inflamed skin drags the problem out.

What if wax really is the problem? Lying on your side and putting 2 to 3 drops of olive or almond oil in the ear, three or four times a day for three to five days, softens a build-up so it falls out over about two weeks. Skip drops entirely with a perforated eardrum.

None of this means avoiding pools or headphones altogether - a few changes to drying and cleaning habits usually make the biggest difference. If pain, swelling, or discharge doesn't improve within a couple of days, it's worth seeing a doctor, since a more established infection may need prescription drops. This article is for general information only and isn't a substitute for medical advice.
